title: Achieving Agent Visibility Across the Enterprise
summary: The five questions an agent investigation runs, in order, and the evidence source for each: CloudTrail's 90 days, Entra's seven, Workspace's six months, and the Slack field with nowhere to put an agent.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**The constraint on an agent investigation is not tooling. It is the shortest retention window among the systems you have to join, and for most enterprises that window is seven days.**


Microsoft Entra keeps audit and sign-in logs for seven days on the free tier and 30 days on P1 and P2. CloudTrail's console Event history holds 90 days and only management events. Google Workspace keeps its audit logs six months. Microsoft 365's unified audit log defaults to 180 days. Those four numbers decide which questions are answerable before anyone opens a tool.


The common fix is another dashboard or wider retention, which makes the haystack bigger without making the needle findable. NIST's own incident-response profile is blunter about what is needed: CSF outcome DE.AE-03, "Information is correlated from multiple sources", rated High priority.


We are not arguing for one all-seeing platform. No single tool sees a procurement agent's SaaS call, its ERP write and its Slack post. Some of them cannot even represent the agent: Slack's audit log says an actor "will always be a user on a workspace".


So do two things. Pick the identifier you will correlate on, then write down the order of questions you will run against it. Check your shortest retention window first, because that is the real deadline.


The order, run against one agent identifier every time: **identity** (which agent, acting for whom), **authorization** (what it was allowed to do), **tool calls** (what it actually did), **credential** (which key carried it), **record** (does the story hold together). Each step filters the next, and each has a different evidence source with a different expiry.
